newsitem.title: ITALY: UN food agency claims reform progress.
newsitem.headline: UN food agency claims reform progress.

text.p: The director-general of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) frankly acknowledged on Wednesday his agency's reputation as a big bureaucracy without a clear mission, but insisted the situation had improved.
FAO, housed in a Fascist-era complex near Rome's ancient Colosseum, has been singled out as an example of U.N. excesses.
One of its biggest critics has been its biggest donor, the United States, which has withheld contributions to the U.N. and agencies such as FAO as it pushes for institution-wide reform.

Director-general Jacques Diouf, of Senegal, told a news conference called specifically to discuss reform that his efforts to streamline the agency and focus its mission had resulted in savings of almost $25 million in the 1996-97 budget.
He said the agency's 1996-97 budget is $650 million, while the 1994-95 budget had been $673 million.

These savings had been realised through cutting 456 jobs from a staff of 4,185 and other cost-controlling measures such as less travel, fewer and shorter meetings, fewer publications and shorter documents, the agency said.

A FAO statement distributed at the news conference noted "past organisational weaknesses, including a centralised, cumbersome bureaucracy and a lack of focus" and said FAO had been "radically changed".
Diouf, who has headed the agency since 1994, ran for the office on a reform platform and has made decentralisation one of his main missions, moving staff from Rome to field offices.

"FAO has had to reform itself becuase the world has changed. What was right 30 or 50 years ago isn't right any more," he said, noting the end of the Cold War, market globalisation and advances in information technology.
Diouf said he did not know whether the budget cuts would be enough to convince the U.S. to pay the $95 million it owes FAO for past contributions.

"We have not had these discussions with the U.S.," he said. "What I have read in the newspapers is that the Clinton administration has requested from Congress $100 million to pay the U.N., the FAO included."
"The U.S. was pleased with many of the changes (at FAO)...Naturally some would like for us to do even more, to cut our budget even more," Diouf added.

The United States has cited the slow pace of U.N. reform as the main reason for vetoing the re-election of Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. secretary-general. Instead it supported Kofi Annan of Ghana, who was sworn in last December.

FAO was founded some 50 years ago with the mission to help the world feed itself. It researches issues relating to nutrition, agriculture, fisheries and forestry and disseminates the information to its 174 member countries.
